newsitem.title: UK: Suspect killed as police foil IRA bomb plot.
newsitem.headline: Suspect killed as police foil IRA bomb plot.

text.p: Police shot dead a suspected IRA guerrilla during a series of dawn raids on Monday and seized up to 10 tonnes of home-made explosives that foiled an imminent vehicle bomb attack in mainland Britain.

The discoveries crushed hopes the IRA might be preparing to call a new ceasefire. Police arrested five people in London and southern England and also seized three Kalashnikov rifles, two handguns, two trucks and an array of bomb-making equipment.

"I have no doubt that today's operation has frustrated an attempt by the Provisional IRA to carry out significant and imminent attacks on the mainland with the possibility, indeed the probability, of grave loss of life, serious damage and disruption to mainland cities," Sir Paul Condon, London's police chief, told a news conference.
Condon's assistant, David Veness, said he could not rule out the possibility that the IRA was planning to launch an attack as early as Monday or Tuesday -- with London a likely target.

The last Irish Republican Army attack, in the northern English city of Manchester in June, injured more than 200 people with a lorry bomb estimated to contain 1.5 tonnes of explosive -- less than a sixth of Monday's haul.
Monday's raids followed a carefully planned operation involving the security services as well as 10 regional police forces that had lasted several weeks.
As well as finding ready-to-use explosives, police discovered at least two bombs designed for fixing under cars, which Veness described as classic Provisional IRA devices.
Condon declined to say whether the man who was shot was himself armed. The suspected guerrilla died in hospital of his wounds. No one else was injured.

Speculation has been rife over the past 10 days that the IRA was about to reinstate its ceasefire -- a move that would allow its political wing, Sinn Fein, to take part in all-party peace talks about a political settlement for Northern Ireland.
But Prime Minister John Major said the raids put speculation about a new IRA ceasefire into "proper context".
"It remains impossible to reconcile Sinn Fein's rhetoric for peace with the IRA's preparations for murder," Major said.
The IRA, which seeks a united Ireland, dramatically ended a 17-month-long ceasefire in February with a half-tonne bomb in London's Docklands commercial area that killed two.
Citing what it called British intransigence in a peace process brokered by the Dublin and London governments, the IRA has since planted seven other bombs on the British mainland.

Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said he presumed the bomb cache belonged to the IRA, adding: "Sinn Fein expresses our regret, as we have done in other tragic cases, to the family of the person who was killed."
Condon said police were not linking the planned attacks to Britain's political conference season, which started on Monday with the annual meeting of the centrist Liberal Democrats.

One of the IRA's biggest successes was its bombing of the Brighton hotel housing then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her entire cabinet during the 1984 Conservative Party conference. Thatcher was unharmed but five people were killed.
Politicians and security experts said Monday's find suggested the IRA was stepping up its campaign.

"We are in an era of pretty major IRA activity. It is good news the explosives and bomb-making equipment were found but bad news they were there in the first place," said Professor Paul Rogers of Bradford University.

Former U.S. congressman Bruce Morrison, who helped broker the September 1994 IRA ceasefire and who had talks with Sinn Fein in Belfast on Saturday, said: "It is certainly a disturbing development in the extreme and I guess it underscores the seriousness of getting to a truly a peaceful situation."
